KEY MESSAGE 1...Showers through the evening, perhaps a rumble of 
thunder.

A fairly dynamic system, the bulk of which is passing by well to our 
north, will be the forcing mechanism to bring the chance of showers, 
and perhaps a brief rumble of thunder, to portions of the area late 
this afternoon through late evening. Hi-res CAMs are not capturing 
very well the cluster of stronger convection across parts of Ontario 
into central New York, so confidence in the evolution and timing of 
any showers that make it into southern New England is on the lower 
side. The convection appears to be primarily elevated, and mid-
level lapse rates across our area are progged to be marginal to 
maintain some of the activity. With no specific model doing well 
with the current activity, I stuck with the blended guidance 
approach, showing 30-40% PoPs in a general WNW to ESE orientation 
from western MA down to SE MA and the Cape and points north of that. 
Rainfall amounts should be generally 1/4" or less, though up to 1/2" 
is possible, especially across far northern areas closer to the 
VT/NH borders.  Otherwise lots of low clouds, and some fog along the 
coast courtesy of a moist low level southeast flow.  As the evening 
and overnight goes on, the winds will transition to southwest and 
start to bring some drying to the low levels. So after any showers 
move through, we should start to see partial clearing prior to 
sunrise. On the flip side, those clouds will keep low temperatures 
from dropping too much. In fact, some areas might see a slow rise in 
temperatures. 

KEY MESSAGE 2...Mild and breezy day Wednesday. Low chance for an
isolated shower or sprinkle in the afternoon. Dry conditions 
Thursday with seasonably cool temperatures.

A trailing cold front shifts across the region Wednesday with 
surface high pressure slowly building in from the west through the 
day. This will gradually clear out the lower clouds through the 
morning. Model soundings show sufficiently mixed supporting drier 
conditions and breezy westerly winds. Gusts likely range between 20-
30 mph with a locally higher gust in the higher terrain of the 
Berkshires. Westerly, downslope flow combined with 925mb 
temperatures +16-18C will support a warm fall day with highs in the 
70s in many areas. Isolate shower are possible as a weak wave moves 
through in the afternoon, but this will be fairly limited in 
coverage and more likely limited to a sprinkle due to the drier 
lower levels. 

As high pressure settles in further into Thursday, the airmass dries 
out even more. Thursday will likely be dry, although cooler than 
Wednesday. A cooler airmass will have moved in with 925mb 
temperatures around 10C cooler than Wednesday. This will yield 
seasonably cool temperatures mainly in the low 60s and lighter 
northerly winds. 


KEY MESSAGE 3...Low pressure system expected to bring rain
Friday into early Saturday. Gusty northwest winds and below 
normal temperatures expected Saturday behind the system. 

Deterministic and ensemble guidance show a deep northern stream 
shortwave trough push across the Great Lakes and the northeast 
Friday into Saturday. An upper level jet setting up near southern 
New England will provide support for broad synoptic ascent and 
advect a plume of anomalous moisture into the region. This will set 
the stage for a widespread rain. Ensemble guidance ranges amounts 
generally from 0.30 to 0.80". The ECMWF and Canadian still lean 
wetter than the GFS despite its subtle upward trend in amounts. The 
wetter solutions show potential for banded or localized amounts of 
1.0-1.4", likely a result of the additional frontogenetical forcing 
combined with marginal instability. Location of where the bands of 
heavier amounts set up is still uncertain. Rain most likely arrives 
in the Friday morning timeframe, continuing through the evening. 
Most guidance shows this system to be fairly progressive meaning it 
shifts out fairly quickly. The bulk of the rain likely exits late 
Friday night with the pre-frontal trough. There is also an axis of 
instability associated with this trough which may provide enough 
forcing/support for a line of convective showers and perhaps even a 
thunderstorm in the mix. 

In addition, the initial southerly LLJ with this system nudges in 
Friday which if mixed sufficiently, will bring breezy to gusty SW 
winds. Gusts 20-35 mph are possible with potential for gusts up to 
40 for the Cape and Islands and also Block Island. 

A strong cold front pushes across the region by early Saturday 
morning putting the northeast within a classic cold air advection 
pattern with gusty NW winds, cooler temperatures, and isolated 
showers. A NW 30-40 kt 850mb jet pushes into the region Saturday. 
CAA will provide the steeper lapse rates to support deeper mixing 
and thus gusty NW winds. The degree or mixing and strength of the 
LLJ are still less certain this far out, but ensembles show a signal 
for gusts 35-45 mph possible,
